# [2026] QIC (F) 75

In the name of His Highness Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Emir of the State of Qatar
Neutral Citation: [2026] QIC (F) 75 IN THE QATAR FINANCIAL CENTRE CIVIL AND COMMERCIAL COURT FIRST INSTANCE CIRCUIT
Date: 3 November 2026
CASE NO: CTFIC0011/2026

DWF LLP (QATAR BRANCH) v
QATAR BUILDING COMPANY WLL

Claimant Defendant

JUDGMENT
Before: Justice Dr Georges Affaki



Order 1. The Claimant’s application for anonymisation is granted in the terms recorded in this
judgment.
2. The Claimant’s application for the proceedings to be sealed is dismissed. 3. The Claimant’s claim in respect of unpaid fees succeeds. Accordingly, the Defendant
is ordered to pay the Claimant QAR 4,147,277 in respect of the 38 invoices listed in paragraph 49.
4. The Defendant is ordered to pay the Claimant simple interest at 5% per annum on the amounts outstanding under those invoices, accruing after one calendar month has elapsed from the date of each outstanding invoice, until payment.
5. The Defendant’s counterclaims for unjust enrichment and damages are dismissed, save for nominal damages in the amount of QAR 20.
6. The Claimant is entitled to recover from the Defendant 70% of its reasonable and proportionate costs of these proceedings, the amount of these costs to be assessed by the Registrar if not agreed between the parties within 14 days of the date of this Judgment.
7. The Defendant must pay to the Claimant the amounts in paragraphs 3 and 4 above, less the QAR 20 awarded under paragraph 5 above, within 21 days of the date of this judgment.
8. The Defendant must pay to the Claimant the amount in paragraph 6 above no later than 21 days after the date of the parties’ agreement on that amount or the Registrar’s assessment of that amount.

Introduction

Judgment

1. This judgment concerns a claim for unpaid professional fees brought by DWF LLP (Qatar Branch), the QFC branch of a limited liability partnership incorporated in England and Wales and registered in the QFC (the ‘Claimant’ or ‘DWF’), against its former client Qatar Building Company JLC, a construction company registered in

2



Qatar (the ‘Defendant’ or ‘QBC’). The claim concerns a total of 38 invoices.
2. In accordance with this Court’s decision to grant the Claimant’s application for the anonymisation of third parties and non-essential details of the underlying arbitrations, this judgment will refer to the matters that are the basis of the Claimant’s claim for unpaid fees by using, where necessary, the coding suggested by the Claimant in its Skeleton Argument at paragraphs 12 and 16.5, and agreed by the Defendant at the hearing.
3. On 21 April 2026, the Claimant commenced legal proceedings against the Defendant before this Court, seeking an order for the Defendant to pay:
i. QAR 4,053,617 under 33 unpaid invoices, together with 6.5236% annual interest from the due dates of those invoices until the date of payment, for legal work done in relation to the S, AG, DR, ETC and AE disputes;
ii. costs; and iii. any other relief as appropriate. 4. On 12 July 2026, the Defendant filed its Statement of Defence and Counterclaim, asking the Court to:
i. dismiss the Claimant’s claims; ii. declare that the Claimant has breached its contractual and fiduciary duties; iii. order a “full accounting between the parties”; iv. order the Claimant to pay QAR 5,200,000 by way of restitution of
overpayments;
v. order the Claimant to pay damages amounting to QAR 5,000,000; and vi. order the Claimant to pay its costs and interest on any sum awarded. 5. On 2 August 2026, the Claimant filed its Reply to Defence and Counterclaim, seeking, in addition to the sums already sought in its Statement of Case, payment of QAR 93,660 for five additional invoices issued between 24 April 2026 and 28 May 2026 relating to work undertaken in the DR, AG and S disputes, plus 6.5447% annual interest from the due dates of those invoices until the date of payment.
3


6. On 9 August 2026, the Court issued an order directing that requests for disclosure pursuant to article 27.2.2 of the Rules and Procedures of the Court (the ‘Rules’) should be made by 16 August 2026, and witness statements filed by 3 September 2026.
7. No request for disclosure was submitted by either party. On 3 September 2026, the Claimant submitted Mr Kirk Durrant’s witness statement.
8. On 16 September 2026, the Defendant uploaded, without notice, a new document to the eCourt platform for inclusion as evidence in the hearing bundle.
9. On 17 September 2026, the Defendant sought permission to submit an additional written submission.
10. On 20 September 2026, the Registrar refused the Defendant’s application to file and serve a further submission and the Defendant’s application for additional documents to be admitted in evidence. The Registrar directed that, as a result of the rejection of the Defendant’s application for the inclusion of new evidence, those documents “may not be referred to in the skeleton argument”.
11. On 17 September 2026, the Claimant uploaded the hearing e-bundles. 12. On 24 September 2026, the parties served skeleton arguments. 13. On 26 September 2026, the Claimant submitted an application to exclude or strike out
the Defendant’s skeleton argument on the basis of the Defendant’s introduction of new evidence, new allegations and defences, and failure to cross-reference the hearing bundles.
14. On 6 October 2026, a public hearing took place. 15. At the hearing, both parties were represented, with Simon Hale KC acting for the
Claimant and Ahmed Al Mushiri for the Defendant. Mr Durrant was cross-examined by counsel for the Defendant and answered questions from the Court based on his witness evidence.
The factual background 16. The material factual background may be summarised as follows.
4


i. On 17 December 2018, the Claimant, the Defendant and another company (‘C’) entered into a letter of engagement (the ‘LoE’). The initial instructions were to advise and represent the Defendant and C in preliminary jurisdictional challenges in two arbitrations commenced against them by S and AN respectively, arising out of the same construction project in Qatar.
ii. Between 17 December 2018 (the date of conclusion of the LoE) and 11 April 2026 (the date of its termination), the Claimant provided legal services to the Defendant across 17 matters. The invoice bundle contains 44 invoices issued before termination: the 33 invoices forming the original claim and 11 historical invoices supplied for context. It also contains the five further invoices issued after termination and added to the claim.
iii. On 13 July 2023, the Claimant’s Managing Partner, Mr Kirk Durrant, asked Mr Hossam Abu Al Ola, QBC’s Group Legal Counsellor, whether the Defendant had any objections to DWF advising certain entities on a dispute against a joint venture involving other entities. The Defendant replied with a voice message that “Actually, we don’t have participants in this JV […] we have no issue at all advising [L’s parent company].”
iv. On 4 and 5 January 2025, Mr Durrant and Mr Abu Al Ola exchanged proposals concerning fee write-offs, discounts and caps for closed and ongoing matters. Negotiations continued thereafter. Further agreement was reached on 21 April 2025, although the fee caps for the AG and DR disputes remained to be agreed and were subsequently settled.
v. On 30 January 2025, the Secretariat of the International Court of Arbitration of the International Chamber of Commerce (‘ICC’) notified the Defendant of ICC arbitration proceedings commenced by another entity (‘L’), represented by the Claimant, against the Defendant and another party as co-respondent.
vi. On 21 December 2025, the Claimant submitted its statement of account, listing unpaid legal fees for seven matters in relation to which the Claimant indicates it had been instructed by the Defendant. The statement of account issued by the Claimant showed a total of QAR 7,331,453.18 of unpaid fees.
5


vii. On 30 December 2025, the Defendant issued a bank instruction to transfer QAR 3,000,000 to the Claimant in “partial settlement for statement of account dated 21/12/2025.”
viii. On 31 December 2025, Mr Abu Al Ola sent a WhatsApp voice note to Mr Durrant, in which, following reference to the anticipated receipt by the Defendant of funds from an external source, he confirmed that the “remaining value” under the outstanding invoices would be “paid before 30 March”.
ix. On 24 February 2026, Mr Durrant sent a WhatsApp message to Mr Abu Al Ola, asking him to confirm whether “we are still good for full payment end of March”. On the same day, Mr Abu Al Ola replied “I’m doing payment now. After transferring will see the remaining value and give you acceptable plan”. Upon a further WhatsApp message enquiry from Mr Durrant on the same date on whether “the plan will still conclude all payments by end of March”, Mr Abu Al Ola replied “This is my plan until now. But delaying mp case might put me in critical pass but I will manage as priority so we can be ok by end of March”.
x. On 16 March 2026, the Claimant issued a statement of account to the Defendant showing a total outstanding amount of QAR 5,430,765.18 due under five matters: “the S dispute”, the “DR dispute”, the “AG dispute”, the “AE dispute”, and the “ETC dispute”.
xi. On 30 March 2026, Mr Durrant sent a WhatsApp message to Mr Abu Al Ola asking him to confirm: […] that you are aware that we (DWF) are acting for [the arbitration claimant] on the Road Settlement Arbitration in which the QBC/ […] joint venture is on the other side and that QBC has no objection to us acting for [the arbitration claimant] in that matter? I know you already confirmed this verbally but our compliance folks need a confirmation in writing […]. Mr Abu Al Ola replied […] Yes confirmed. I will do.
xii. On 4 April 2026, the Defendant shared with the Claimant a copy of a SWIFT transfer message relating to a payment of QAR 1,638,363.18 to the Claimant. On 5 April 2026, the Claimant thanked the Defendant for “sorting this payment
6


and for sending across the swift transfer” and confirmed that the payment had been received.
xiii. On 8 April 2026, the Claimant informed the Defendant that the amount of QAR 1,638,363.18 had been allocated to DWF’s oldest invoices and provided an updated statement of account showing total outstanding fees of QAR 4,053,617 incurred in relation to the S, AG, DR, ETC and AE disputes. In the same email, the Claimant stated:
We would be grateful if you could kindly provide an update on the payment status on our QBC following matters. We would appreciate settlement of the outstanding invoices within this month. Your assistance in resolving these matters is greatly appreciated. We look forward to hearing from you.
xiv. By letter dated 11 April 2026 (the ‘Termination Letter’), the Claimant terminated the LoE: … in accordance with Clause 4(g) of the Terms […] due to the continued non-payment of very long outstanding fees, which currently total QAR 4,053,617 per the enclosed statement of Account dated 8 April 2026. In the letter of termination, the Claimant noted that: for the avoidance of doubt, we will cooperate with any lawyers appointed by you in relation to the prompt transfer of files if so directed by you.
xv. On 12 April 2026, the Claimant wrote to the Defendant offering:
… to assist with an orderly transition in relation to: (i) the ongoing setaside applications in respect of the [S dispute] final award before the QICDRC; and (ii) the [AG dispute] arbitration.
xvi. In relation to the S proceedings, the Claimant noted its understanding that the Defendant was in the process of finalising a settlement with S and that, once concluded, the Defendant would discontinue both set-aside applications by sending the draft email provided by the Claimant to the Court. In relation to the AG arbitration, the Claimant recalled that the arbitration was suspended until 30 June 2026 to allow the parties to have their settlement agreement notarised.
xvii. By separate email on that same date, the Claimant wrote to the Defendant offering “to assist with an orderly transition of the [DR dispute] and [AE dispute] arbitrations”. The Claimant enclosed a “very advanced (near-final) draft of the Respondent’s costs submission” to be filed in the DR dispute
7


arbitration and noted that both closing and costs submissions had already been filed in the AE dispute arbitration, thus leaving “no steps envisaged at this time”.
xviii. Between 24 April 2026 and 28 May 2026, the Claimant issued five additional invoices relating to work undertaken in the DR, AG and S disputes before and immediately after the termination of the LoE.
Analysis
17. I shall first address the Claimant’s applications concerning anonymisation and the exclusion of the Defendant’s skeleton as preliminary issues. Second, I shall consider the Claimant’s claim for payment and interest. Third, I shall determine the Defendant’s counterclaims for declaratory relief, restitution and damages, then proceed to allocate the parties’ costs.
18. The jurisdiction of this Court and the law applicable to these proceedings are not in dispute. Clause 18(j) of the Terms of Business (the ‘Terms’) attached to the LoE provides as follows:
These terms shall be governed by and interpreted in accordance with QFC law and any claim arising out of any matter we handle for you shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the QFC Courts (save in relation to the enforcement of any judgment obtained by us against you). Each party irrevocably waives any right it may have to object to an action brought in those Courts, to claim that the action has been brought in an inconvenient forum, or to claim that those Courts do not have jurisdiction.
19. The Court has jurisdiction under article 8.3(c)(4) of Law No. 7 of 2005, as amended (the ‘QFC Law’), and article 9.1.1.4 of the Rules, the dispute arising from a retainer between an entity established in the QFC and an entity established in the State outside the QFC. Clause 18(j) confirms the parties’ submission to this jurisdiction and their choice of QFC law. The QFC Contract Regulations 2005 (the ‘Contract Regulations’) accordingly apply.
Preliminary issues
The Claimant’s application for these proceedings to be anonymised and sealed
20. The Claimant asks that these proceedings be anonymised and sealed, pursuant to paragraphs 2 and 5 of Practice Direction No. 1 of 2023 (Access to Documents and Confidentiality), to protect the confidentiality of the arbitration proceedings
8


referenced in the pleadings. At the hearing, the Defendant confirmed that it did not object to the proceedings being anonymised.
21. In the present circumstances, the anonymisation of the identity of third parties and other details regarding these arbitrations that are not otherwise central to the dispute is a proportionate measure which would not detract from the proper understanding of the case and I therefore see no obstacle in granting it. I have, however, found no sufficient reasons for the court file to be sealed and, in the interests of the principle of open justice, the Claimant’s application for these proceedings to be sealed is dismissed.
The Claimant’s application for certain paragraphs of the Defendant’s skeleton to be excluded 22. The Claimant avers that certain paragraphs in the Defendant’s skeleton amount to a late attempt to introduce new factual allegations and supporting evidence without leave from the Court, which would, if admitted, prejudice the Claimant.
23. Accordingly, the Claimant requests the Court to strike out the following paragraphs from the Defendant’s Skeleton Argument:
i. paragraphs 12(a), 13 to 23, which concern new allegations of professional negligence and breach of contractual obligations arising out of the AE dispute arbitration;
ii. paragraphs 12(c), 31 to 37, and 49 to 54, which concern new allegations on the purported lack of authority of Mr Abu Al Ola to represent the Defendant; and
iii. paragraphs 38 to 56, which concern new developments on the alleged conflict of interests arising out of the Claimant’s representation of L in an arbitration against the Defendant.
24. The Claimant avers that these matters should have been pleaded in the Defendant’s Statement of Defence and Counterclaim in accordance with Chapter 7.6 of the User Guide (the Maroon Book). The Claimant further notes that the purpose of the skeletons, as noted in Chapter 17.2 of the Maroon Book, is to identify those points which are, and are not, in issue, and the nature of the argument in relation to the points in issue.
9


25. At the hearing, in reply to a question from the Court, the Defendant explained that the late introduction of these new defences and counterclaims was the consequence of counsel being instructed only after the submission of the Defendant’s Statement of Defence and Counterclaim, and of new elements coming to light after the submission of the Defendant’s Statement of Defence and Counterclaim. The Defendant also acknowledged that it had not sought leave to amend its Statement of Defence and Counterclaim and that its requests for permission to file additional pleadings and new evidence had been rejected by the Registrar as untimely.
26. In determining this matter, I first note article 4.5 of the Rules, which provides that “It is the duty of the parties to any case before the Court to assist the Court in determining that case in accordance with the Overriding Objective”.
27. Article 4.1 of the Rules clarifies that the “Overriding Objective of the Court is to deal with all cases justly”, which includes, pursuant to article 4.3, ensuring that litigation before the Court takes place expeditiously, that the parties are treated on an equal footing, and that the case is dealt with in a manner proportionate to the financial stakes and the complexity of its legal and factual matrix.
28. Chapter 17.2 of the Maroon Book provides as follows: A skeleton argument is intended to identify both for the parties and the Court those points which are, and are not, in issue, and the nature of the argument in relation to the points in issue.
29. It is common ground that the paragraphs of the Defendant’s skeleton argument identified by the Claimant include new factual allegations and grounds of defence and counterclaim extending beyond those advanced in the Defendant’s Statement of Defence and Counterclaim. Those new matters were first advanced on 24 September 2026, a mere 12 days before the date of the hearing. On their face, these new developments were not, at the time of the simultaneous filing of the parties’ respective Skeleton Arguments, “points in issue”.
30. Admitting these out-of-time developments at such a late stage would require to reopen proceedings to afford the Claimant an opportunity to respond. This would counter the imperatives of dealing with the case expeditiously and proportionately. The Defendant has not provided credible excuses for the late introduction of new evidence and legal grounds of defence and counterclaim, that would justify disrupting the orderly 10


determination of the proceedings.
31. In the exercise of the Court’s case management powers under articles 15.1 and 15.2 of the Rules, and having regard to the Overriding Objective, I direct that the Defendant be barred from relying on paragraphs 12(a), 13 to 23, 38 to 48, 55 to 56 of its skeleton argument. This does not prevent the Defendant from relying on paragraphs 12(c), 31 to 37, and 49 to 54 of its skeleton argument to the extent that the substantive allegations in those paragraphs have been voluntarily and properly addressed, to the Court’s satisfaction, by the Claimant at the hearing and can therefore be adjudicated without jeopardising the Claimant’s right to be treated on an equal footing with the Defendant in accordance with article 4 of the Rules.
The Defendant’s request for an accounting reconciliation between the parties Background
32. The Defendant asks the Court to direct “a complete accounting between the Parties” because the duration of the relationship, the numerous matters involved, the multiple fee arrangements and the Claimant’s “disputed billing methodology” require an independent accounting exercise to determine whether the Claimant was overpaid.
33. The Claimant objects on the grounds that the Defendant’s objective is to delay the adjudication of the dispute. It submits that the Defendant has not identified duplications, accounting errors, reconciliation discrepancies or irregularities in the Claimant’s account.
Analysis and Decision 34. The Defendant has approached this request in abstract terms. Whilst in its pleadings it complains in general terms about the Claimant’s billing methodology and points to a potential risk of overpayment, it has failed to identify a single billing or reconciliation discrepancy that would warrant ordering the requested accounting exercise. Any such measure is bound to bring about cost and delay that would be disproportionate to the issues requiring determination. As such, it goes against the Overriding Objective of the Court to deal with all cases justly, as indicated in article 4 of the Rules.
35. The Defendant’s request for an accounting reconciliation is therefore dismissed.
11


The Claimant’s claim for outstanding legal fees Background
36. The Claimant claims outstanding fees under 38 invoices, amounting in total to QAR 4,147,277, comprising QAR 1,606,109.07 for S, QAR 1,244,603 for DR, QAR 804,504.93 for AG, QAR 61,360 for ETC and QAR 430,700 for AE, with contractual interest at a rate ranging from 6.5236% to 6.5447%, from the due date of the invoices until payment is made in full by the Defendant.
37. The Defendant objects to the payment of the fees claimed by the Claimant on the three following grounds.
38. The first ground is based on the characterisation of the contractual relationship between the Claimant, the Defendant and C as one of “joint professional retainer”. This ground need not be examined further as the Defendant, at the hearing, confirmed that it withdrew this ground of defence in light of clause 4(b) of the Terms, which enables DWF to recover from either QBC or C the full amounts of charges due:
Where we are instructed by more than one person jointly, liability for our charges, disbursements and, if applicable, any sales taxes that are in force from time to time (Sales Taxes), is shared between those persons on a joint and several basis so that we may recover from any one or more of those persons individually or together the full amount of our charges, disbursements and any Sales Taxes notwithstanding any agreement which may be reached between those persons.
39. The second ground is that, according to the Defendant, the Claimant’s invoices are not sufficient to establish liability and, accordingly, the Claimant has failed to satisfy its burden of establishing that the claimed amounts are due.
40. The third ground is that the financial position presented by the Claimant is “incomplete and unreliable” and fails to account for all the payments made by the Defendant.
41. The first ground of defence having been withdrawn, I turn directly to the Defendant’s second ground. The Claimant counters that it is undisputed that DWF provided legal services to QBC in connection with the disputes. Pursuant to clause 10 of the LoE, the Defendant was required to pay DWF’s invoices within 30 calendar days of their first issue. The Claimant avers that the Defendant never questioned those invoices or otherwise disputed its liability. Instead, on several occasions, and as late as 24
12


February 2026, the Defendant made express commitments to pay the entire debt by certain dates but failed to act accordingly.
42. In the Claimant’s view, the issue between the parties was never whether the Defendant was liable to pay the invoices. Rather, the Defendant attributed its failure to make timely payment to cashflow difficulties, which the Claimant attempted to accommodate through fee capping, invoice and time write-offs, and discounts, all of which were accepted by the Defendant. To that end, the Claimant notes that it was only after the termination of the relationship between the parties on 11 April 2026 that the Defendant began treating the claimed fee amount as disputed.
43. As to the third ground of defence, the Claimant notes that every invoice claimed in these proceedings was accompanied by a detailed schedule evidencing the completed work. During the parties’ more than seven-year relationship, the Defendant never raised a complaint, continued instructing the Claimant on new matters, and repeated its commitment to pay outstanding fee amounts. Moreover, the Claimant notes that when seeking to recover the Claimant’s fees from the other parties in multiple arbitrations, the Defendant represented to arbitral tribunals that those costs were reasonable, justified and recoverable, a position which the Defendant should not now be entitled to recant.
Analysis and Decision 44. The Claimant relies on the following provisions:
i. Article 95 of the Contract Regulations, which provides as follows: Where a party who is obliged to pay money does not do so, the other party may require payment.
ii. Clause 10 of the LoE, which provides as follows (as is material): We will bill on a monthly basis. We will provide you with information about how our charges have been calculated. Payment of invoices must be made within 30 calendar days of when they are first issued […]
iii. Clause 4(e) of the Terms, which provides as follows: Unless specific terms of payment have been agreed, bills, whether interim or final, should be settled upon receipt. Interest may be charged on bills that are not paid on time at 2.5% above 1 (one) month QIBOR, as published by Qatar Central Bank from time to time,
13


after one calendar month has elapsed from the date of the bill until payment.
45. Having reviewed the claim in light of the second ground of defence, I view this matter as a straightforward debt claim despite the apparent complexity of the facts due to overlapping legal service matters and parallel disputes. It is common ground that the Claimant rendered legal services to the Defendant from December 2018 to April 2026 across multiple matters. Invoices for legal services were issued and paid, albeit intermittently and not in full, thereby generating a backlog of rolling indebtedness.
46. Whilst write-offs, discounts and other arrangements to facilitate payment by the Defendant were agreed from time to time, those arrangements were part of the ordinary course of a business relationship between a client and a legal service provider. I found no evidence that the Claimant’s invoices were inflated, or that the work carried out had not been authorised. The absence of evidence that the Defendant ever took issue with the Claimant’s work before the termination of the LoE is relevant in that regard. The original fee cap agreed in the LoE concerned the preliminary jurisdictional challenges in relation to the S dispute and the AN dispute, rather than all subsequent work done for the Defendant in the several matters it entrusted to the Claimant. Later fees were governed by the parties’ revised arrangements and charged in accordance with clause 8.3 of the LoE, providing that “in the event of additional or alternative services being provided [to those described in the LoE], then additional or alternative charges may be incurred.”
47. Regarding the third ground of defence, the Defendant has not provided particulars to support its argument that the financial position presented by the Claimant in support of its claim is either incomplete or unreliable, that the work billed was unnecessary, or that the invoices do not reflect the work actually undertaken. No serious doubt has been cast as to whether the Claimant provided legal services to the Defendant. The Defendant itself, in the costs submissions that it filed towards the conclusion of the DR arbitration, represented the Claimant’s invoices as being reasonable, echoing identical statements made in the AE, ETC and S arbitral proceedings. Whilst the burden remains on the Claimant to establish its contractual entitlement and the amount due on the balance of probabilities, that does not require proof of a separate instruction for every time entry. On the other hand, the detailed work schedules, contemporaneous instructions and payment records must be considered together with the Defendant’s
14


contemporaneous conduct. Taken together, I am satisfied that, on a balance of probabilities, the Claimant succeeds in establishing its entitlement to the claimed fees as the adduced evidence adequately supports its claim (see Zahir Makawy v Al Awael Captive Insurance Company LLC [2024] QIC (F) 11, paragraph 12). The Defendant’s general, unsubstantiated and unparticularised objections do not displace the Claimant’s proof of entitlement. Indeed, the Defendant has failed to build a credible case on the two remaining grounds upon which it relies to deny its liability, namely, the contention that the invoices should not suffice to establish a debt, and the alleged unreliability of the financial position supporting the Claimant’s claim.
48. Whilst the five additional invoices issued on 24 April 2026, 27 April 2026 and 28 May 2026 include post-termination work for the DR, AG and S disputes, I accept the Claimant’s assertion that the invoiced work was limited to necessary steps undertaken to protect the Defendant’s position in the disputes, for instance the finalisation of costs submissions that would enable the Defendant to recover its costs in the arbitral proceedings and the drafting of emails setting out the immediate next steps for winding the proceedings down. The related fees are therefore recoverable pursuant to clause 3(m) of the Terms.
49. Therefore, I find that the Claimant is entitled to full payment for the fees it claims in these proceedings. Accordingly, the Defendant is ordered to pay the Claimant all outstanding amounts under the following 38 invoices in relation to the S, AG, DR, ETC and AE disputes, as detailed below, totalling QAR 4,147,277:
